name: Mark Broadie
one_line: The Columbia Business School quant-finance professor who invented "strokes gained" and, in doing so, rewrote golf's understanding of what actually wins tournaments.
bio: Broadie is an operations researcher by training — B.S. from Cornell, Ph.D. from Stanford — who joined Columbia Business School in the early 1980s and built a substantial academic career in quantitative finance, best known for foundational work on Monte Carlo simulation methods for pricing American and path-dependent options (much of it with Paul Glasserman) and for exact simulation of stochastic-volatility models. A serious recreational golfer, he began in the early 2000s collecting shot-by-shot data on amateur rounds through software he wrote called Golfmetrics, then gained access to the PGA Tour's ShotLink laser-tracking database when the Tour opened it to academic researchers in 2007. Applying dynamic programming and benchmarking logic borrowed from finance, he built the strokes gained framework, which the Tour adopted as Strokes Gained: Putting in 2011 and later extended to full tee-to-green categories; his 2014 trade book Every Shot Counts brought it to the public and became the field's founding text. He is now the Carson Family Professor of Business (and a former Vice Dean), designed the ranking algorithm the Official World Golf Ranking adopted in August 2022, consults for tour pros, coaches and broadcasters, and is a fixture at the MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference.
known_for: Inventing "strokes gained" — measuring each shot against a field-average benchmark for the same starting position
Every Shot Counts (2014), the foundational popular text of golf analytics
Demolishing "drive for show, putt for dough": showing the long game, especially approach shots, explains most scoring differences among pros
Showing that driving distance is worth more than driving accuracy, a finding later invoked by Bryson DeChambeau and the modern power era
Golfmetrics, his amateur shot-tracking database and app, and the resulting diagnosis that amateurs lose most strokes on the long game
Designing the Official World Golf Ranking algorithm used since August 2022

Academic quantitative finance: Boyle–Broadie–Glasserman (1997) survey of Monte Carlo methods for security pricing; Broadie–Glasserman simulation methods for American options; Broadie–Kaya exact simulation of affine stochastic-volatility processes
school: Operations research and decision analysis under uncertainty — the Stanford/Columbia OR tradition of dynamic programming, simulation and stochastic modeling — applied to sport in the sabermetric mold.
lineage: Methodologically he descends from Bellman-style dynamic programming and the Monte Carlo/computational finance school he helped build with Paul Glasserman at Columbia; conceptually he is golf's Bill James, arriving after Moneyball made benchmark-relative performance measurement respectable. In golf he supersedes an older empirical line — Cochran and Stobbs's Search for the Perfect Swing, Peter Sanders's early performance analytics, and above all Dave Pelz, whose claim that putting and the short game dominate scoring Broadie's data directly contradicted. His descendants are everywhere in the modern game: Scott Fawcett's DECADE course-management system, Lou Stagner's popular data writing, Data Golf's modelling, shot-tracking consumer products like Arccos and Shot Scope, tour-side analytics groups, and the broadcast vocabulary of Golf Channel and Sky, all of which take strokes gained as the base unit of account.
stance: Golf performance should be measured the way a portfolio is measured — against an appropriate benchmark, shot by shot — rather than by the traditional box-score stats (fairways hit, greens in regulation, putts per round) that conflate skill with circumstance and answer no useful question. Once you do that, the received wisdom collapses: putting accounts for only about 15 percent of the scoring advantage of the best pros, approach play is the single largest factor, distance beats accuracy off the tee, and for amateurs the fastest route to lower scores is a better long game and fewer catastrophes, not a magical short game. Strategy, too, is a solvable expected-value problem: given your own dispersion pattern, aim to maximize expected strokes gained rather than to imitate what looks brave or prudent. Underneath the golf, his claim is general — good decisions under uncertainty come from measuring the right thing against the right baseline.
blind_spots: Strokes gained is accounting, not causation: it is zero-sum against a field baseline, so it describes who gained strokes and where, without explaining why, and it cannot separate good decisions from lucky outcomes — a reckless shot that comes off scores well. Its category-level numbers are noisy over small samples, and critics note that ShotLink baselines smooth over context (lie quality, wind, pin position, green slope, rough severity), which the earliest putting version handled crudely. His most famous popular conclusion — that distance dominates accuracy — has been widely read as blanket license to hit driver, when it is a Tour-level, average-conditions result that can invert on narrow, penal setups; his strategic prescriptions also assume a risk-neutral expected-value maximizer and sit uneasily with match play, tournament situation, and the psychology of real players. The amateur half of his argument rests on a smaller, self-selected Golfmetrics sample than the Tour half, though later consumer-tracking datasets have largely corroborated it. The single most contested item on his record is public rather than academic: the OWGR algorithm he designed drew sustained complaints after 2022 from LIV Golf, DP World Tour and secondary-tour players over how field strength is computed and how opaque the system feels from outside. Stylistically, Every Shot Counts is often described as chart-heavy and repetitive — a reference work more than a narrative.
politics: No discernible political orientation in the public record. His public writing, teaching and interviews are confined to quantitative finance, analytics methodology and golf; he does not appear to comment on partisan or ideological questions, and nothing in the available material supports an inference either way. Treat him as effectively apolitical in public. The only quasi-political terrain he has entered is golf-industry governance — his OWGR ranking work placed him near the PGA Tour/LIV Golf dispute — and even there he has spoken as a technician about methodology rather than taking sides.
public_views: "Drive for show, putt for dough" is simply wrong; the long game explains roughly two-thirds of scoring differences among professionals
Approach shots are the biggest single differentiator in elite golf; putting is a much smaller share of the advantage than folklore holds
Distance off the tee is more valuable than fairways hit — the penalty for missing a fairway is usually smaller than the gain from being closer
Traditional golf statistics are close to useless for diagnosis because they ignore where a shot started and where it finished
Amateurs misallocate practice: they lose most strokes on the long game and to blow-up holes, not on the putting green
Course strategy should be built around your own shot dispersion — aiming at conservative targets, often the middle of the green, is usually the higher-expected-value play
Data should inform how a player allocates practice time, not replace coaching or feel
The strokes gained idea generalizes: performance measurement in business is only managerially useful when it is relative to the right benchmark
Sports data will keep expanding, and the value lies less in new numbers than in putting them in context
interview_notes: Unfailingly professorial and mild-mannered — journalists reach for words like understated and soft-spoken. He is a myth-buster without swagger: he hedges carefully, says "on average" a lot, resists the sweeping soundbite even when interviewers hand him one, and repeatedly frames himself as a golfer who wanted to know how to improve his own game before he was a golf researcher. Recurring themes across podcasts (Chicago Golf Report, North Star), CNN and Irish Times profiles, and his Sloan Sports Analytics Conference appearances: the uselessness of legacy stats, the primacy of approach play, the distance-versus-accuracy result, the importance of avoiding disasters, and the transferability of benchmark-relative measurement to business. He enjoys telling the story of DeChambeau name-checking him in a US Open winner's press conference, and he leans on shot-pattern visuals rather than equations when speaking to golf audiences. He is generous about other analysts and notably uninterested in personal brand-building.
